m1_00_opening: For Euphemia Haynes, mathematics was never merely a collection of calculations.
She wrote that mathematics is no more the art of reckoning and computation than architecture is the art of making bricks, or painting the art of mixing colors.
But mathematics begins when we discover the structure that joins them.
m1_01_reason: A correct answer was not enough.
Haynes wanted the student to discover why a statement is true.
He understands it, he will retain it for it is his belief.
The difference is the difference between receiving an answer and constructing an idea for oneself.
m1_02_inquiry: Her classroom ideal was active: observation, experimentation, construction, reflection, and then another look.
A mathematical object could be changed, tested, and examined from another direction.
Learning meant participating in the mathematical process rather than watching it from outside.
m1_03_constant_variable: Haynes also used mathematical concepts as ways of thinking.
Some features of a problem remain fixed while others change.
The important question is not simply what changed, but what the change allows us to see.
m1_04_relationships: Mathematics is also a study of relationship and dependence.
Change one quantity and another responds.
The emphasis shifts from isolated facts toward connections, consequences, and structure.
m1_05_freedom: And then there is dimension: the number of independent directions in which movement is possible.
A point has no freedom of motion.
On a line it gains one direction.
On a plane it gains another.
This gives us a visual metaphor for the larger promise of education: knowledge can open paths that were previously closed.
Mathematics can become an open door.
